Q: Is injecting the MainPage into an app and registering it as a singleton a recommended approach in .NET MAUI? A:

I can give you some information about your questions 2 (Should MainPage be registered as a singleton, or would be using transient more appropriate?) and 3 (Are there any lifecycle, navigation, memory-management, or multi-window issues with keeping a singleton MainPage). The reality is that even the guys who drive this platform may turn out to be clueless about it.

If you read docs, you may come across this:

For most .NET MAUI use cases:

  • Use AddTransient<T> for pages and view models to get a fresh instance on each navigation.

  • Use AddSingleton<T> for shared services such as database connections, settings, or caches.

Which is pretty much what we knew all along. It is logical. Pretty much non-optional for MAUI's original - Xamarin. Original shell needed to be able to re-create new page when needed, and managed the life cycle internally.

You do not follow this rule - runtime exception. This is what I do ever since MAUI came along. Apps in Appstore/Google play, everything works fine. I am using shell navigation, however.

The interesting situation is that despite the docs stating "transient for pages", "singleton for services", taking a look at what examples the MAUI team provides to you - you will notice that they do EXACTLY THE OPPOSITE.

One page above you see transient service, followed by singleton main. Then one page below you see how they make extension methods to register both the view models and the views as singletons, and the services as transient.

At some point (honestly no idea when), the situation for double-registering routes and changing from transient to singleton changed. It doesn't seem to be causing crashes. And you will most likely not encounter any lifetime related issues, no matter what you do.

Your best bet is good end-to-end tests, now and every time you upgrade your MAUI workload and community toolkit. This is the current best practice.

Q: How do I sync my local repository to a GitHub repo? A:

First you need to run

git remote -v

in the root of your versioned folder. You should see your GitHub repo, something like

<remote>    <yourpath> (fetch)
<remote>    <yourpath> (push)

You can push to the remote via

git push <remote> <branch>

or, if <name> happens to be origin, then you can simplify to

git push

if the branch is properly resolved.

Now, if you have lots of changes, you can add your changes via:

git add file1
git add file2
git add file3

or all of them as

git add .

and then commit

git commit -m "your message"

as many times as you wish. Doing a

git push

every once in the while should not become a huge problem, but if you may forget doing it, then you could make git push being triggered automatically, see here.

Or, if you have loooots of big changes and it takes a lot of time to push, then you could create an automatic job scheduled for the time of your lunch break to do a git push, in Linux that would be a cron job.

Q: Langgraph Studio Multi-Agent Example: Hierarchical Agents? A:

The main trick with LangGraph Studio for hierarchical multi-agent setups isn’t changing anything special in the Studio UI itself; Studio just visualizes whatever compiled graph you export via your langgraph.json config.

If your sub-agents aren't collaborating or passing context properly, it’s usually because the state isn't flowing through a supervisor router pattern or subgraphs.

In a standard hierarchical setup (supervisor + worker agents), you typically define a shared top-level AgentState with a message list and a next field. You create a "supervisor" node (using structured output / tool-calling to decide which worker to call next) and route to individual worker nodes (or compiled subgraphs).

Each worker executes its task, appends its result to the shared message history, and returns execution to the supervisor node until the supervisor outputs FINISH (which routes to END). Once you export that top-level compiled graph in your langgraph.json

Studio will automatically render the entire multi-node supervisor topology and allow you to inspect the state at each agent handoff.

Q: django.db.utils.NotSupportedError: MariaDB 10.11 or later is required (found 10.6.22) A:

That version mismatch is the key clue: Django 6.1 raised its minimum required MariaDB version to 10.11, and the error is telling you the server your app actually connected to reports 10.6.22 — not the 12.3.3 you installed. So this isn't a Django or mysqlclient version problem, it's that your app is talking to a different MariaDB server than the one you think you're running.

1. Compare TCP vs socket connections

bash

mysql -h 127.0.0.1 -u root -e "SELECT VERSION();"
mysql -u root -e "SELECT VERSION();"

If these return different version numbers, you have two servers running — one reachable via TCP, one via the local socket — and Django is hitting the wrong one.

It's common to still have an old mariadb@10.6 formula installed and running as a background service alongside a newer mariadb. brew services list will show if both are registered, and which one is actually active on port 3306.

3. Check what mysqlclient is actually linked against

Even in a fresh venv, mysqlclient connects via whatever socket path is either configured in your Django DATABASES (OPTIONS: {'unix_socket': ...}) or baked in at build/link time. Check which client library it's actually using:

bash

python -c "import _mysql; print(_mysql.__file__)"
otool -L $(python -c "import _mysql; print(_mysql.__file__)") | grep maria

If it's linked against the Homebrew Cellar path of the old MariaDB version, that's your answer — it needs to be rebuilt against the new one.

4. Unlink the old version and relink the correct one

bash

brew services stop mariadb@10.6   # or whichever old formula you have
brew unlink mariadb@10.6
brew link mariadb                 # link the 12.3.3 install

Then reinstall mysqlclient so it links against the currently active MariaDB client libs:

bash

pip uninstall mysqlclient
pip install --no-cache-dir mysqlclient

The otool -L output and the TCP-vs-socket version comparison are usually what nail it down — 10.6.22 is very likely a leftover Homebrew-managed MariaDB instance quietly still running, not an actual problem with your Django or mysqlclient setup.
